response.question: Someone is selling products with my registered trademark on them. What can I do?
response.answer:
Selling products with your registered trade mark may be infringement, but it is not automatically so. For example, infringement can occur when someone without permitted use sells goods under an identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to goods covered by your registration. Reselling genuine goods is not automatically infringement. The law makes allowances for goods lawfully acquired and put on the market by you or with your consent. There can be exceptions, such as when the goods’ condition has changed or been impaired. [trade_marks_act_1999:30]

If your registration is valid, you may seek relief for infringement, subject to the conditions and limitations of your registration. A trade mark lawyer can help assess the facts and discuss your options. [trade_marks_act_1999:28]

response.question: Can I sue someone for using my brand name if I never registered it?
response.answer:
Yes, you may be able to bring a “passing off” suit even if you never registered your brand name. Passing off can protect an unregistered trade mark used in business. The law recognises suits where someone uses a mark identical to, or so similar to, yours that it is likely to deceive or cause confusion.

Whether you have a case depends on the facts. The court may grant an order stopping the use and, in some cases, damages or an account of profits. These outcomes are not guaranteed. A passing off suit must be brought in a court no lower than a District Court with jurisdiction.

response.question: Why could my trademark application be rejected?
response.answer:
Your application could be refused for several reasons, depending on your mark and the goods or services it covers:

- The mark does not distinguish your goods or services from someone else’s; it only describes them, or it consists only of terms commonly used in the trade. There is an exception if, before you applied, the mark had become distinctive through use or was well known. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
- It could deceive or confuse the public, hurt religious sensitivities, contain scandalous or obscene matter, or be prohibited under the law on emblems and names. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
- It consists only of certain shapes: for example, a shape necessary to achieve a technical result. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
- It is identical or similar to an earlier mark, and the marks and goods or services are sufficiently alike to create a likelihood of public confusion. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]
- It is identical or similar to an earlier mark that is well known in India, even for different goods or services, if using it without due cause would unfairly benefit from or harm the earlier mark’s distinctiveness or reputation. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]
- Its use could be prevented by copyright law or by passing off law, which can protect an unregistered mark used in business. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

The last two grounds require an objection by the earlier mark’s proprietor in opposition proceedings. Consent from the owner of the earlier mark or right can also be relevant; registration is not automatic. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

The Registrar may refuse an application or accept it with conditions or changes. If it is refused or accepted conditionally, the Registrar must record the reasons and supporting material in writing. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

response.question: How long is a trademark registration valid and how do I renew it?
response.answer:
A trade mark registration under the current Act lasts for 10 years and can be renewed for further 10-year periods. For a registered mark, the registration date is generally the application date, subject to exceptions. [trade_marks_act_1999:25; trade_marks_act_1999:23]

To renew, the registered owner must apply to the Registrar in the prescribed manner, within the prescribed period, and pay the prescribed fee. The sources provided do not specify the form, fee amount or ordinary filing window. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

If the registration has expired, an application in the prescribed form with the fee and surcharge can be made within six months of expiry. If the mark has been removed for non-payment, the owner can apply for restoration after six months and within one year of expiry, with the prescribed fee. Restoration depends on the Registrar being satisfied that it is fair to restore it. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

response.question: How long does copyright last for a book after the author dies?
response.answer:
In India, copyright in a book published during the author’s lifetime generally lasts for 60 years, counted from 1 January of the year after the author’s death. For example, if the author died in 2020, the 60 years run from 1 January 2021 to the end of 2080.

For a jointly authored book, the period generally runs from the year after the last author dies. Different rules can apply if the book was first published after the author’s death, or was published anonymously or under a pen name.

response.question: My employer says they own the articles I wrote at work. Who owns the copyright?
response.answer:
It depends on your job, why you wrote the articles, and any agreement you made.

If you wrote them in the course of your employment under a contract of service, your employer is generally the first copyright owner, unless you agreed otherwise. [copyright_act_1957:17]

There is a special rule if you worked for a newspaper, magazine or similar periodical and wrote the articles for publication in one. Unless you agreed otherwise, the proprietor is the first owner of the rights to publish or reproduce them for publication in such periodicals; you are the first owner of the other copyright rights. [copyright_act_1957:17]

The author is generally the first owner, subject to exceptions such as these. Copyright can also be transferred wholly or partly, so an agreement may affect who owns which rights. [copyright_act_1957:17] [copyright_act_1957:18]

response.question: What is the jail punishment for copyright piracy?
response.answer:
For knowingly infringing copyright, the usual punishment is 6 months to 3 years in jail, plus a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. This also applies to knowingly helping someone infringe copyright.

If the infringement was not for gain in the course of trade or business, the court may impose a shorter jail term or a lower fine, but must give special reasons in its judgment.

For a second or later conviction under this provision, the usual jail term is 1 to 3 years, plus a fine of ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh. A similar exception allows the court to impose a shorter term or lower fine where the infringement was not for gain in trade or business.

A separate rule applies to knowingly using a pirated computer program: the usual punishment is 7 days to 3 years in jail, plus a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. If it was not used for gain or in trade or business, the court may, for special reasons, impose no jail sentence and a fine of up to ₹50,000.

response.question: Can someone challenge or oppose my patent?
response.answer:
Yes. Someone can oppose a patent application or challenge a granted patent, but the available routes depend on the stage:

• Before grant: Once your application is published, any person can oppose the grant in writing to the Controller, the patent authority. [patents_act_1970:25]

• A granted patent can also be challenged through a request to the High Court to revoke it, meaning cancel it. An interested person or the Central Government can make such a request. A challenge can also be raised in response to a patent infringement suit. [patents_act_1970:64]

Opposition grounds include, for example, that the claimed invention was published earlier, was obvious, or was not clearly and sufficiently described in the patent document. The law lists the permitted grounds; an opposition cannot be based on an unrelated ground. [patents_act_1970:25]

For a post-grant opposition, the Controller notifies the patent owner, obtains recommendations from an Opposition Board, and gives both sides a chance to be heard. The Controller then decides whether to keep, amend or revoke the patent. [patents_act_1970:25]

response.question: What exclusive rights does copyright give me over my novel?
response.answer:
If you own the copyright in your novel, you have the exclusive right to do the following things, or authorise someone else to do them, with the novel or a substantial part of it [copyright_act_1957:14]:

- Reproduce it, including storing it electronically.
- Issue copies to the public, other than copies already in circulation.
- Perform it in public or communicate it to the public.
- Make a film or sound recording based on it.
- Translate it or make an adaptation, such as a shortened version or a dramatic version [copyright_act_1957:2].
- Exercise these rights in relation to a translation or adaptation of the novel.

These rights are subject to limits in the law. For example, certain fair dealing for private or personal use, including research, is not infringement [copyright_act_1957:52].

Separately, as the author, you have the right to claim authorship and to seek to stop or claim damages for certain changes that harm your honour or reputation, even if you have assigned the copyright [copyright_act_1957:57].

response.question: Is it a crime to sell fake branded goods?
response.answer:

Another defence applies if they prove that, when asked by or on behalf of the prosecutor, they gave all the information they had about their supplier.

The punishment is generally six months to three years in prison and a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. For adequate and special reasons recorded in its judgment, the court may impose a lower prison term or fine.

response.question: Can another company force me to let them make my patented medicine?
response.answer:
Yes, in some circumstances—but another company cannot simply decide to force you to let it make your medicine. It may apply for a compulsory licence, which is permission granted by the Patent Controller without needing your agreement. The Controller decides whether to grant it. [patents_act_1970:84]

For a usual compulsory-licence application, an interested person must wait until three years after the patent was granted. The grounds include unmet public requirements, an unaffordable price, or the invention not being worked in India. The Controller also considers whether the applicant tried unsuccessfully to obtain a licence on reasonable terms; that consideration does not apply in certain situations, including a national emergency or extreme urgency. [patents_act_1970:84]

When setting the licence terms, the Controller must endeavour to ensure that any royalty or other payment is reasonable and that the licence is non-exclusive, meaning it does not give the licensee sole rights. [patents_act_1970:90]

A separate compulsory licence can be granted to manufacture and export a patented medicine to a country with insufficient or no manufacturing capacity for it, to address public health problems. The destination country must have granted a compulsory licence or otherwise allowed the import. [patents_act_1970:92A]

response.question: A company copied my patented invention. What can a court order against them?
response.answer:
In a patent infringement suit, a court may order:

- An injunction: an order directing the company to stop the infringing activity.
- Either damages (money for loss) or an account of profits (a remedy based on profits made from the infringement), at your choice.
- Seizure, forfeiture or destruction, without compensation, of goods found to be infringing. The court may also make such an order for materials and tools used predominantly to create those goods.

The court decides what relief to grant. Money remedies have limits: for example, they cannot be granted if the company proves that, at the time of the infringement, it did not know and had no reasonable grounds to believe the patent existed. This restriction does not affect the court’s power to grant an injunction.

response.question: How long does copyright protection last in India?
response.answer:
Copyright duration depends on the type of work and when it was published. Many terms are 60 years, counted from 1 January of the year after the relevant event.

• Books, plays, music and artistic works published during the author’s lifetime: generally 60 years from the start of the year after the author’s death. For joint authors, count from the year after the last author dies. [copyright_act_1957:22]
• Films and sound recordings: 60 years from the start of the year after publication. [copyright_act_1957:26] [copyright_act_1957:27]
• Anonymous works and works published under a pen name: generally 60 years from the start of the year after first publication. If the author’s identity is disclosed before that term expires, the period is instead counted from the year after the author’s death. Joint authorship has additional rules. [copyright_act_1957:23]
• Certain works first published after the author’s death: 60 years from the start of the year after first publication, subject to conditions. An earlier publication of an adaptation can affect the calculation. [copyright_act_1957:24]
• Government works and public-undertaking works: where the government or public undertaking is the first copyright owner, 60 years from the start of the year after first publication. [copyright_act_1957:28] [copyright_act_1957:28A]
• Certain international organisations’ works: 60 years from the start of the year after first publication. [copyright_act_1957:29]

Foreign works may be subject to an order that limits their term in India. [copyright_act_1957:40]

response.question: Can I patent a software application or mobile app idea in India?
response.answer:
Possibly, but not simply because you have an app idea. Indian patent law excludes a computer programme “per se” (by itself), as well as mathematical methods, business methods and algorithms [patents_act_1970:3].

An invention involving software is not necessarily excluded just because it involves software. Whether your particular invention can be patented depends on what you are seeking to protect. The available sources do not explain exactly where the boundary around a programme “per se” lies.

Other issues also matter: an application can be opposed if the claimed invention was published before the relevant date, or if it is obvious and lacks an inventive step—a non-obvious contribution [patents_act_1970:25].

Separately, copyright law includes computer programmes as literary works and sets out rights relating to their reproduction [copyright_act_1957:2; copyright_act_1957:14]. Copyright and patents protect different things.

response.question: Can my product's packaging or colour scheme be protected as a trademark?
response.answer:
Yes. Your product’s packaging or combination of colours may qualify as a trade mark if it can be represented visually and can distinguish your goods from those of others. Registration is not automatic. [trade_marks_act_1999:2]

A trade mark can be limited to a combination of colours; that limitation is considered when deciding whether the mark is distinctive. A mark registered without a colour limitation is treated as registered for all colours. This does not mean every use of those colours by someone else is automatically prohibited. response.question: My neighbour filed a police complaint accusing me of stealing his expensive laptop. I have CCTV footage proving that I was not even present at his house that day. What can I do against a false criminal complaint? Can I take legal action against him?
response.answer:
Yes, legal action may be possible, but it depends on the facts. Your CCTV footage may help challenge the theft accusation. It does not by itself establish that your neighbour knew or believed his complaint was false.

Under section 217, giving a public servant information known or believed to be false may be an offence if the required intent or knowledge about the likely misuse of the official’s powers is also present. This could be relevant to a false police complaint. [bns_2023:217]

There may also be a possibility of compensation. If a case triable by a Magistrate reaches that court and you are discharged or acquitted, the Magistrate may consider compensation if satisfied there was no reasonable ground for the accusation. The complainant must be given an opportunity to explain. Compensation is not automatic. [bnss_2023:273]

The available sources do not explain the full procedure for bringing action against your neighbour. A lawyer can assess your options.

response.question: Police officers came to my house and arrested my brother without explaining the reason. They have not allowed us to contact a lawyer or informed us about where he is being taken. What are his legal rights after arrest, and what can our family do?
response.answer:
I’m sorry your family is facing this. The rules depend partly on whether the police used an arrest warrant, which is a court order to arrest someone.

• If your brother was arrested without a warrant, the police must promptly tell him the full details of the offence or other grounds for arrest. If the alleged offence is bailable, they must also tell him he can be released on bail and arrange sureties—people who provide the required assurance for his release. [bnss_2023:47]
• The arresting officer must promptly inform a relative, friend or other person your brother names about the arrest and where he is being held. The officer must also inform the designated district police officer. At the police station, your brother must be told of this right, and the station must record who was informed. [bnss_2023:48]
• If police interrogate him, he can meet a lawyer of his choice during questioning, although the lawyer need not be present throughout. [bnss_2023:38]
• The arresting officer must display clear identification and prepare an arrest memorandum—a record of the arrest—witnessed and countersigned as required. [bnss_2023:36]
• He must be medically examined soon after arrest. The examination record must note any injuries, and a copy must be given to him or someone he nominates. [bnss_2023:53]
• If he was arrested under a warrant, he must be brought before the relevant court without unnecessary delay. The delay cannot exceed 24 hours, excluding necessary travel time. The supplied sources do not establish a general time limit for every other kind of arrest. [bnss_2023:78]
• When he is produced before a Magistrate, the Magistrate must check whether he was told about his right to have someone informed and whether the police recorded who was informed. [bnss_2023:48]

response.question: Three people attacked me while I was walking home at night. I hit one of them with a nearby object to escape, and he suffered serious injuries. Can I claim the right of private defence under Indian criminal law? Could I still be arrested?
response.answer:
I’m sorry you were attacked. You may be able to claim private defence, but whether it applies depends on the circumstances. The law allows a person to defend their body against an offence affecting the body [bns_2023:35].

The right can extend to causing harm short of death, but it does not allow more harm than was necessary for defence. It also does not apply where there was time to seek protection from public authorities [bns_2023:39] [bns_2023:37]. What you reasonably feared, what happened during the attack and whether the harm was necessary are therefore important. Something done within the right of private defence is not an offence [bns_2023:34].

The available sources do not explain the rules for arrest, so I cannot say whether you could be arrested.

response.question: Someone posted false allegations about me on Instagram, claiming that I committed fraud. The post has damaged my reputation and affected my professional opportunities. Can I file a criminal defamation case in India? What remedies are available?
response.answer:
Yes. You may consider a criminal defamation complaint about the Instagram post. A published allegation can amount to defamation if it concerns you and was made intending to harm your reputation, or with knowledge or reason to believe it would do so. Harm can include lowering your professional standing in the eyes of others. Whether the post meets these conditions depends on the facts. [bns_2023:356]

The law also provides exceptions. For example, an allegation that is true and published for the public good is excepted. An allegation made in good faith to protect someone’s interests or for the public good may also be excepted. The court would assess the facts and any applicable exception. [bns_2023:356]

As the affected person, you may make a complaint before a Magistrate who has authority to hear the case. [bnss_2023:222]

If defamation is established, the possible punishment includes simple imprisonment of up to two years, a fine, both, or community service. A fine is not necessarily compensation to you. [bns_2023:356]

The supplied sources do not explain whether you can obtain compensation or a court order to remove the post. You can ask a qualified lawyer about those options.

It does not cover every private photograph, and a threat to leak alone is not one of the acts it lists.

Which provisions apply will depend on the facts.

If an officer refuses to record information about a cognizable offence, you may send it in writing by post to the concerned Superintendent of Police. If that does not resolve the matter, you may apply to a Magistrate. [bnss_2023:173]

The time limit is generally three months from the incident, or three months from the last incident in a series. The committee may extend it by up to three more months if it is satisfied that circumstances prevented you from filing in time, and records its reasons in writing. If you cannot write the complaint, a committee officer or member must give reasonable assistance. [posh_act_2013:9]

response.answer:

Section 3 covers abuse of a Scheduled Caste member by caste name in a place within public view. It also covers stopping a Scheduled Caste member from using common resources or a water source such as a well, water tap or other watering place. These provisions apply where the person responsible is not a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe. Whether they apply in your case depends on the facts [sc_st_atrocities_act_1989:3].

The Act also says the State must arrange protection for victims, their dependents and witnesses against threats or violence [sc_st_atrocities_act_1989:15A].

response.question: The police station near my house refused to register my FIR, saying the incident happened in another area's jurisdiction. Are they allowed to do that?
response.answer:
No—not solely because the incident happened in another area, if the information relates to a cognizable offence. You can give that information to the officer in charge of a police station regardless of where the offence occurred. [bnss_2023:173]

A cognizable offence is one for which police may arrest without a warrant. The facts you have given do not establish whether your case is cognizable. [bnss_2023:2]

If the officer in charge refuses to record information about a cognizable offence, you may send it in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police concerned. If that does not resolve the matter, you may apply to a Magistrate, a judicial officer. [bnss_2023:173]
